lesson.title: haben or sein? Choice Gym
lesson.subtitle: Twenty past-sentence prompts — motion vs transitive logic decides

hook.title: Two Auxiliaries, One Question
hook.content: Every German Perfekt sentence asks one question before anything else: did you DO something to something, or did you GO somewhere? Do → haben. Go → sein. Ich habe gegessen (I ate something) versus Ich bin gegangen (I went). Ich habe das Buch gefunden versus Ich bin nach Berlin gefahren. English solved this problem by abandoning sein-pasts entirely; German kept the ancient perfect-of-motion, and so did English once — 'he is come' is authentic Early Modern English, straight out of the King James Bible.

footnotes.title: He Is Come
footnotes.content: 'He is risen', 'The hour is come', 'Joy cometh in the morning' — the KJV uses be-perfects exactly like German sein-perfects. English narrowed them to phrases of arrival and change; German still runs the whole system: sein with gehen, kommen, fahren, aufstehen, einschlafen, bleiben.

pattern.title: The Decision Tree
pattern.content: Branch one: is there a direct object (something acted on)? → haben, always: Ich habe den Kaffee getrunken. Branch two: motion or change of state with no object? → sein: Ich bin gekommen, Wir sind gegangen, sie ist eingeschlafen (she fell asleep — a change of state). Branch three: the sneaky verbs — bleiben (stay) and sein itself take sein despite zero motion: Wir sind zu Hause geblieben. When in doubt: 'could I do it TO something?' haben. 'did I move or change?' sein.
pattern.linguist_note: Some verbs flip meaning with the auxiliary: Ich habe das Auto gefahren (I drove the car — transitive) versus Ich bin gefahren (I traveled — motion). The auxiliary is doing grammar work, not decoration.

exercises.explanation: gehen is pure motion, no object: sein. English's own KJV said 'he is gone' the same way. ankommen and fliegen ride sein too — arrivals and flights are motion.

exercises.prompt: 'Ich ___ das Buch gelesen.' (I read the book — lesen hinted: to read)
exercises.meaning: Ich habe das Buch gelesen = I read the book
exercises.explanation: Direct object (das Buch) → haben, no debate. Doing something to something is haben territory — buchen takes its object the same way: Ich habe alles gebucht.

exercises.prompt: Match each Perfekt sentence with its auxiliary logic:
exercises.target_answer: Ich bin gekommen, Ich habe gegessen, Wir sind geblieben, Ich habe das Auto gefahren
exercises.meaning: I came, I ate, we stayed, I drove the car
exercises.explanation: Motion → sein; object → haben; bleiben always sein; gefahren flips by whether something was driven. The verb decides: fliegen flies (sein), tragen carries (haben).

exercises.prompt: Complete with the auxiliary: 'Sie ___ eingeschlafen.' (she fell asleep — change of state)
exercises.meaning: Sie ist eingeschlafen = She fell asleep
exercises.explanation: einschlafen is a change of state (awake → asleep) — sein territory, like 'he is fallen' in old English.

exercises.target_answer: Ich bin gestern nach Berlin gefahren

vocab_hints.note: nach Berlin — the 'to' of destination; cities and article-free countries take nach (nach Deutschland)

exercises.explanation: No object driven — just travel: sein. 'Ich bin gefahren' is 'I am come' with wheels.

summary.outcome: Choose haben or sein correctly across transitive, motion, and sneaky-verb cases.

use_example.german: Ich bin gestern nach Berlin gefahren.

summary.takeaway: Object → haben; motion or change → sein; bleiben always sein — the KJV's 'he is come' logic, still living.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: Gestern habe ich… Story Drills — narrate a whole weekend in Perfekt sentences from taught words.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — build in German: "We have here today"
twist.explanation: Building "Wir haben heute hier" from the lesson's core pattern locks in haben or sein? Choice Gym.

essen.shift_rule: T → S / SS / Z + Ablaut Vowels
essen.context_translation: What do we want to eat?
essen.etymology_derivation: Medial t → ss. Noun: das Essen (food).

fahren.context_translation: I am going / driving to Berlin.
fahren.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *faraną — the twin of English fare (farewell, bus fare, 'how did you fare?'). [wiktionary]

trinken.context_translation: I drink a glass of water.

fliegen.context_translation: We are flying to Rome tomorrow.
fliegen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *fleuganą (PIE *plewk-) — English fly is the documented cognate; strong verb: flog, geflogen. [wiktionary]

ankommen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *anakwemana, to come to — an + kommen, with archaic English oncome as the listed cognate. [wiktionary]

buchen.context_translation: I am booking a hotel online.
buchen.etymology_derivation: From Buch plus -en (the beechwood-carving word); the modern reserve sense was modelled after English to book — a semantic loan the page documents. [wiktionary]

tragen.etymology_derivation: Class 6 strong verb from Proto-Germanic *draganą (to carry, drag) - the twin of English draw and drag; tragen-trug-getragen matches draw-drew-drawn. [wiktionary]

notruf.context_phrase: Im Notruf sagt man Name und Adresse.
notruf.context_translation: In the emergency call you say name and address.
notruf.etymology_derivation: Not (need, distress — twin of English need, Proto-Germanic *naudiz) plus Ruf (call); literally need-call — dial 112 or 110. [wiktionary]

chinesisch.etymology_derivation: From the noun Chinese plus the suffix -isch, the twin of English -ish, which the page itself matches to English -ese. [wiktionary]

flug.context_phrase: Unser Flug geht um sieben Uhr.
flug.context_translation: Our flight leaves at seven o'clock.
flug.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *flugiz, the noun of the fly-verb family (fliegen, to fly); the same flug- stem that gives English flight. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
